moonbase.note: A planned lunar habitat runs at about 30% oxygen and 10.2 psi (E3: challenge text). No solid fuel in this dataset was tested above 22.2% oxygen, and no solid-fuel table here records pressure at all.

gravity.note: This dataset (NASA PSI) contains no partial-gravity combustion data. Partial-gravity flame tests have been run on parabolic flights and a spinning suborbital rocket (LUCI), but their results are not in PSI. The idea that flame spread peaks near lunar gravity is a hypothesis here; NASA's FM2 experiment is designed to test it (E3).

key_insights.headline: Silicone burned on Earth but barely in space
key_insights.detail: All four SAFFIRE-II silicone samples left about 0 cm burned in microgravity; at 1 g two burned completely and one 7.6 cm. Earth testing can misjudge a material in either direction. Caveat: four samples, all near the oxygen limit (21.5-22.1% O2).
key_insights.source: PSI-99 SAFFIRE-II, samples 2-1 to 2-4, burn length columns

key_insights.headline: 7 cool flames recorded in CFI-G
key_insights.detail: CFI-G logged 7 cool flames (regimes PCI-A, PCI-B, PCI-C, PCI-D, PCI-E, PCI-F, PCI-G), all in Butane (30%) at 203 kPa and 38.9-39.9% oxygen. A cool flame burns at low temperature and gives off little light.

key_insights.headline: One material burned out while its neighbour never lit
key_insights.detail: SAFFIRE-II sample 2-7: the PMMA portion was completely consumed while the adjacent Nomex was never ignited.

surprises.title: Silicone burns on Earth but barely in space
surprises.text: In SAFFIRE-II, all four silicone samples left about 0 cm burned in microgravity. In normal gravity, samples 2-1 and 2-4 burned completely and 2-2 burned 7.6 cm; only the thickest (2-3, 1.03 mm) failed in both.

surprises.title: 7 cool flames recorded in CFI-G
surprises.text: CFI-G logged 7 cool flames (regimes PCI-A, PCI-B, PCI-C, PCI-D, PCI-E, PCI-F, PCI-G), all in Butane (30%) at 203 kPa and 38.9-39.9% oxygen. A cool flame burns at low temperature and gives off little light.

surprises.title: One material burned out while its neighbour never lit
surprises.text: SAFFIRE-II sample 2-7: the PMMA portion was completely consumed while the adjacent Nomex was never ignited.

gaps: This dataset has no combustion data at any gravity between microgravity and 1 g. Partial-gravity flame tests exist from parabolic flights and LUCI, but not in PSI.

No solid fuel in the PSI tables was tested above 22.2% oxygen, while a lunar habitat is planned at about 30%. Saffire V and VI (outside PSI) did fly at 26.2-31.0% O2 and 54-71 kPa; see Findings > Beyond PSI.
No solid-fuel table in this dataset records chamber pressure, so no reduced-pressure solid test is recorded.
All SAME-R smoke data comes from heated, non-flaming samples: there are no measurements of smoke from genuine flaming fires.
No tests here cover electronics, wiring insulation, foams or packaging.
BASS (PSI-26) records which samples were burned, but not the conditions or how they ended.
SAFFIRE-III records its two burns' conditions but no burn length, spread rate or burn time.

coverage.pressure_note: No solid-fuel table in this dataset records chamber pressure, so reduced-pressure coverage for solids cannot be shown; none is recorded.

research_questions.question: Do droplet extinction and cool flames behave differently at partial gravity?
research_questions.why: Liquid spills (fuels, solvents, lubricants) are a habitat hazard alongside solids.
research_questions.known: FLEX (274 droplet tests) and CFI-G (179 gas tests) are all microgravity tests.
research_questions.gap: No droplet or cool-flame measurement between microgravity and 1 g.
research_questions.answer_by: A droplet module on a partial-gravity platform.
research_questions.measure: Extinction diameter and burn time of methanol and heptane droplets at 0.16 g.

research_questions.question: Is oxygen partial pressure or oxygen fraction the better predictor of flammability at reduced pressure in microgravity?
research_questions.why: Habitats raise the oxygen fraction while lowering pressure; which of the two controls risk decides the safe operating envelope.
research_questions.known: No solid-fuel table in PSI records pressure. FLEX droplets cover 70-309 kPa.
research_questions.gap: Solids at matched partial pressure but different total pressure.
research_questions.answer_by: A flow-duct test series varying pressure at fixed oxygen partial pressure.
research_questions.measure: Spread rate and extinction limit for the same material at 3 pressures, same O2 partial pressure.

research_questions.question: Does Nomex stay non-flammable in a 30% oxygen, 70 kPa habitat atmosphere?
research_questions.why: Nomex is used for crew clothing and covers; its safety margin at habitat oxygen is unknown.
research_questions.known: Nomex never sustained a flame in microgravity: 3 failed BASS-II attempts at 21-22.2% O2, and it did not ignite next to burning PMMA in SAFFIRE-II sample 2-7.
research_questions.gap: No Nomex test above 22.2% oxygen.
research_questions.answer_by: Saffire-class or SoFIE tests at habitat atmosphere.
research_questions.measure: Ignition and spread of Nomex at 26-31% O2 and 55-70 kPa.

research_questions.question: How do diluents other than nitrogen change solid flammability?
research_questions.why: Diluent choice for habitat air affects both flammability and suppression.
research_questions.known: FLEX tested CO2 (123 tests) and helium (50 tests) only with droplets.
research_questions.gap: No solid-fuel test with CO2 or helium diluents.
research_questions.measure: Extinction oxygen level for PMMA in N2, He and CO2 backgrounds.

research_questions.question: Which materials burn in a suit atmosphere of 100% oxygen at 4.3 psi, at lunar gravity?
research_questions.why: Suit and suitport materials face the most oxygen-rich environment on a mission.
research_questions.known: No investigation in PSI, and none in the literature reviewed here, covers it.
research_questions.gap: Complete absence of data.
research_questions.answer_by: Ground tests in reduced gravity aircraft; FM2-class lunar tests.
research_questions.measure: Ignition and spread of suit fabrics at 100% O2, 30 kPa, 0.16 g.

research_questions.question: How does the low-flow quenching limit change with sample thickness?
research_questions.why: Thick materials dominate the real fuel load of a cabin.
research_questions.known: In BASS-II's notes, thick PMMA slabs went out at 5-18 cm/s, while SIBAL fabric went out below about 3 cm/s; material and flow direction also differ.
research_questions.gap: No single-material thickness series at fixed flow direction.
research_questions.answer_by: BASS-type tests on PMMA of 0.1, 1, 3 and 10 mm in one flow direction.
research_questions.measure: Quenching airflow vs thickness.

research_questions.question: Why did the opposed-flow SAFFIRE-I burn last 70 s while the concurrent one lasted 420 s?
research_questions.why: Flow direction may change fire duration by a factor of six at large scale.
research_questions.known: SAFFIRE-I: sample S1 (concurrent, 20 cm/s) burned 420.0 s; S2 (opposed, 20 cm/s) burned 70.0 s.
research_questions.gap: The table does not record why S2 ended or how far it spread.
research_questions.answer_by: Saffire IV-VI video and reports; repeat tests.
research_questions.measure: Spread distance and extinction cause for opposed large-scale burns.

research_questions.question: How do wire bundles and cable insulation burn in microgravity?
research_questions.why: Electrical faults are the most likely ignition source in a spacecraft.
research_questions.known: No wire or cable sample appears in any of the 14 PSI tables.
research_questions.gap: Complete absence of data in this dataset.
research_questions.answer_by: Saffire-class tests with cable bundles; dedicated wire-insulation experiments.
research_questions.measure: Ignition by overload, spread along insulation, smoke yield.

research_questions.question: How do foams and packaging materials burn in microgravity?
research_questions.why: Cargo bags and foams make up a large share of the combustible mass in a module.
research_questions.known: No foam or packaging sample appears in the PSI tables.
research_questions.gap: Complete absence of data in this dataset.
research_questions.measure: Spread rate, heat release and smoke for common foams.

research_questions.question: How do circuit boards and electronics enclosures burn?
research_questions.why: Electronics combine an ignition source with polymer fuel.
research_questions.known: No electronics sample appears in the PSI tables.
research_questions.gap: Complete absence of data in this dataset.
research_questions.measure: Ignition from overheated components; spread over boards.

research_questions.question: Why did Nomex fail to ignite while the PMMA attached to it burned completely?
research_questions.why: Real assemblies mix materials; one burning material may or may not ignite its neighbour.
research_questions.known: SAFFIRE-II sample 2-7: the PMMA portion was completely consumed, but the Nomex was not ignited (table Note 2).
research_questions.gap: One sample; the heat transfer between the two was not measured.
research_questions.measure: Heat flux at the junction; ignition of the second material.

research_questions.question: Is silicone's reversal (burns at 1 g, barely in microgravity) real away from its oxygen limit?
research_questions.why: If silicone is safer in space only near the limit, the advantage may vanish at habitat oxygen.
research_questions.known: Four SAFFIRE-II silicone samples, all at 21.5-22.1% O2 (near the limit), left about 0 cm burned in microgravity; two burned completely and one 7.6 cm at 1 g.
research_questions.gap: Only four samples, all near the oxygen limit.
research_questions.measure: Microgravity burn length vs oxygen for silicone sheets of several thicknesses.

research_questions.question: Does lunar dust on a surface change how it ignites or burns?
research_questions.why: Dust will coat everything in a lunar habitat.
research_questions.known: DAFT sampled Arizona Road Dust aerosol in 2 sessions; no combustion test included dust.
research_questions.gap: No flammability test with dust-covered samples.
research_questions.answer_by: Ground tests with lunar simulant; FM2-class tests.
research_questions.measure: Ignition delay and spread rate of dusted vs clean samples.

research_questions.question: Why did so many diluted-butane ignition attempts fail in CFI-G?
research_questions.why: Ignition failures mark the edge of flammability, the most informative region.
research_questions.known: 18 of 52 Butane (30%) attempts never ignited.
research_questions.gap: The CFI-G table does not separate igniter problems from true non-flammability.
research_questions.answer_by: Repeat tests with recorded igniter energy.
research_questions.measure: Igniter power and duration for each attempt; flammable or not.

research_questions.question: What ignition energy does a solid need at habitat oxygen levels?
research_questions.why: Sets how hot a fault must get to start a fire.
research_questions.known: SAFFIRE igniters ran at 80, 97, 182 W; BASS-II used several igniter types.
research_questions.gap: No measured minimum ignition energy for solids in microgravity.
research_questions.measure: Minimum ignition energy vs oxygen and airflow.

research_questions.question: Why do flames self-extinguish at steady airflow in microgravity?
research_questions.why: A flame that dies on its own without intervention changes how a crew should respond.
research_questions.known: 7 BASS-II flames went out by themselves at steady flow (M2, M9, M10, M14, M19, O13a, P21a).
research_questions.gap: The cause (oxygen depletion, heat loss, fuel geometry) is not separated.
research_questions.answer_by: Tests with local oxygen and temperature probes.
research_questions.measure: Local oxygen, radiant heat loss and fuel regression at extinction.

research_questions.question: At what droplet size does radiation put out a flame?
research_questions.why: Large spills burn differently from small droplets.
research_questions.known: FLEX recorded visible-extinction diameters from 0.12 to 4.60 mm (median 1.78 mm).
research_questions.gap: Radiative extinction has not been isolated from other causes in the table.
research_questions.measure: Radiant loss and extinction diameter for large droplets.

research_questions.question: What does aged smoke from FLAMING materials look like in microgravity?
research_questions.why: Smoke detectors are tuned to particle sizes; flaming smoke differs from heated-sample smoke.
research_questions.known: All 109 SAME-R tests heated samples without flaming.
research_questions.gap: No microgravity smoke data from real flames.
research_questions.answer_by: A SAME-type experiment with flaming samples.
research_questions.measure: Particle size distribution and aging of flaming smoke.

research_questions.question: Can smoke detectors tell lunar dust from smoke?
research_questions.why: False alarms erode trust; missed fires are worse.
research_questions.known: DAFT measured Arizona Road Dust aerosol; SAME-R smoke particles grew by Rt/R0 = 1.22-1.48 with aging.
research_questions.gap: No test exposed a detector to dust and smoke together.
research_questions.measure: Detector response to dust, smoke and mixtures.

research_questions.question: Which sensor detects an invisible cool flame first?
research_questions.why: A cool flame gives off little light, so optical detectors may miss it.
research_questions.known: CFI-G recorded 7 cool flames; FLEX researchers reported heptane droplets burning on invisibly after visible extinction.
research_questions.gap: No comparison of CO, formaldehyde or infrared sensors on cool flames.
research_questions.answer_by: Cool-flame tests instrumented with candidate sensors.
research_questions.measure: Time to detection for each sensor type.

research_questions.question: How quickly does carbon monoxide build up before a fire is visible?
research_questions.why: CO is both a hazard and a detection signal.
research_questions.known: BASS-II measured CO before and after each burn, with final readings up to 950 ppm (test O13a).
research_questions.gap: Only start and end values; no time history in the table.
research_questions.answer_by: Time-resolved gas sampling in flow-duct tests.
research_questions.measure: CO over time from ignition.

research_questions.question: Does smoke aging time change where detectors should be placed?
research_questions.why: Smoke particles grow as they drift; a detector far from a fire sees different smoke.
research_questions.known: SAME-R aged smoke for up to 1923 s.
research_questions.gap: Link between aging, distance and detector response not established.
research_questions.measure: Particle size at several distances from the source.

research_questions.question: How well does CO2 put out solid fires at reduced pressure and raised oxygen?
research_questions.why: CO2 extinguishers are standard on spacecraft; their margin at habitat conditions is unknown.
research_questions.known: FLEX tested CO2 only on droplets (123 tests). No PSI table tests suppression of solids.
research_questions.gap: No solid-fire suppression data in microgravity at habitat conditions.
research_questions.answer_by: Suppression tests in a flow duct.
research_questions.measure: CO2 concentration needed to extinguish PMMA and SIBAL at 30% O2, 70 kPa.

research_questions.question: Is helium a better suppressant than CO2 at the same concentration?
research_questions.why: Suppressant choice affects mass, toxicity and effectiveness.
research_questions.known: Raw FLEX shares of tests ending in extinction: 80% with helium, 72% with CO2, 57% with neither. These shares mix different oxygen levels and fuels.
research_questions.gap: No controlled comparison at matched oxygen and pressure.
research_questions.measure: Extinction probability vs diluent fraction at fixed oxygen.

research_questions.question: Does water mist work in microgravity?
research_questions.why: Water is plentiful and non-toxic.
research_questions.known: No PSI investigation tested water mist.
research_questions.gap: Complete absence of data in this dataset.
research_questions.measure: Extinction time and mist mass needed.

research_questions.question: Can cutting ventilation be used to put out a fire without filling the cabin with smoke?
research_questions.why: Turning off fans starves a microgravity flame but stops smoke removal.
research_questions.known: Stopping the airflow put out 8 BASS-II flames; 43 went out as flow was turned down.
research_questions.gap: Smoke distribution after ventilation shutdown is unmeasured.
research_questions.measure: Smoke concentration over time after fan shutdown.

research_questions.question: Why did cool flames appear only in one fuel and pressure in CFI-G?
research_questions.why: Knowing where cool flames occur tells designers where to look for them.
research_questions.known: All 7 recorded cool flames were in Butane (30%) at about 203 kPa and 38.9-39.9% O2.
research_questions.gap: Other fuels and pressures produced none in this table; the reason is not established.
research_questions.measure: Cool-flame occurrence across fuels, pressures and oxygen.

research_questions.question: Can vapours from heated cabin materials form cool flames?
research_questions.why: An overheating material might burn invisibly before visible flame appears.
research_questions.known: PSI cool-flame data comes from gas and liquid fuels only.
research_questions.gap: No cool-flame test with pyrolysis vapours from solids.
research_questions.measure: Cool-flame onset temperature for common cabin polymers.

research_questions.question: Do large heptane spills create a cool-flame hazard?
research_questions.why: Liquid hydrocarbons are carried as fuels and solvents.
research_questions.known: 81 FLEX heptane droplets were larger than 2.4 mm, the size range where invisible burning was reported after visible extinction.
research_questions.gap: The FLEX table records visible extinction only.
research_questions.measure: Duration of invisible burning vs droplet size.

research_questions.question: How does a fire grow from glovebox scale to module scale?
research_questions.why: Small tests are cheap; real fires are large.
research_questions.known: BASS-II samples were 1 cm and 2 cm wide; SAFFIRE-I burned a 94 x 40.6 cm sheet.
research_questions.gap: Few intermediate scales to connect the two.
research_questions.measure: Spread rate and flame size vs sample width.

research_questions.question: How long can a large fire burn in a sealed spacecraft?
research_questions.why: Determines how much time a crew has.
research_questions.known: The longest burn in SAFFIRE-I lasted 420.0 s.
research_questions.gap: Duration vs volume and oxygen not characterised.
research_questions.measure: Burn duration and final oxygen in a closed volume.

research_questions.question: How did each BASS (PSI-26) test end, and under what conditions?
research_questions.why: BASS has 122 tests whose outcomes would double the solid-fuel evidence.
research_questions.known: The BASS table records sample and date only.
research_questions.gap: No oxygen, airflow or outcome in the experimental table.
research_questions.answer_by: Transcription from the BASS final report, as done here for BASS-II.
research_questions.measure: Oxygen, airflow, direction and outcome per test.

research_questions.question: What pressure did each solid-fuel test run at?
research_questions.why: Without pressure, reduced-pressure risk cannot be read from existing data.
research_questions.known: No solid-fuel table in PSI records chamber pressure.
research_questions.gap: Pressure missing for all 300+ solid tests.
research_questions.measure: Chamber pressure per test.

research_questions.question: What does the FLEX-2 per-test data show?
research_questions.why: FLEX-2 extends droplet work to more fuels and mixtures.
research_questions.known: Only an 8-row range summary of FLEX-2 is included here.
research_questions.gap: Per-test FLEX-2 results are not in this dataset.
research_questions.measure: Per-test conditions and outcomes.

recommendations.title: Do not approve habitat materials on the Earth upward-burning test alone
recommendations.action: Add a microgravity or low-flow test for any material that will fill a habitat, because the normal-gravity screening test can misjudge it in both directions.

evidence.text: PMMA kept burning in microgravity at 14.8% O2 (BASS-II test O4); attempts at 13.6-14.6% O2 did not sustain a flame.
A separate result for a cellulose fuel (not PMMA): its Earth oxygen limit is 16.5% O2, yet with spacecraft-like ventilation (5-20 cm/s) flames survived at 14% O2.
The other direction: all four SAFFIRE-II silicone samples left about 0 cm burned in microgravity, while two burned completely at 1 g.

recommendations.strength: Strong for PMMA (dozens of BASS-II tests). Weak for silicone: four samples, all near the oxygen limit.

recommendations.title: Test materials at the habitat's own atmosphere before choosing 30% oxygen
recommendations.action: Run flammability tests at about 30% O2 and 70 kPa, and use the Saffire V-VI results, before fixing the habitat atmosphere.

evidence.text: No solid fuel in the PSI tables was tested above 22.2% O2, and no solid-fuel table records pressure.
Saffire V and VI burned samples at 26.2-31.0% O2 and 54-71 kPa in Cygnus, close to habitat conditions.

recommendations.strength: The gap itself is certain (it is a count of what was never tested). What happens inside it is not yet known from PSI.

recommendations.title: Do not assume lunar gravity is safer than orbit
recommendations.action: Screen habitat materials at lunar gravity, and treat 0.16 g as a possible worst case until FM2 and similar experiments report.

evidence.text: LUCI (Blue Origin, 2025): at simulated lunar gravity SIBAL's flame spread more slowly (tip 1.1 vs 2.8 mm/s at 1 g) but burned about 45 s longer before going out.
Related work suggests the oxygen concentration needed for flammability reaches a minimum near lunar gravity.
PSI contains no test between microgravity and 1 g.

recommendations.strength: Early: one sounding-rocket flight with two samples, plus a hypothesis that FM2 (late 2026) is designed to test.

recommendations.title: Shut off ventilation to fight a fire, and confirm it is fully out before turning it back on
recommendations.action: Make it possible to stop air movement quickly in each module, and before ventilation is restored, check that no near-invisible flamelets survive; do not treat slow air as safe.

evidence.text: In BASS-II, 43 flames went out as the crew turned the airflow down and 8 when they stopped it.
Raising the airflow blew 12 flames off.
With flow on the order of spacecraft ventilation (5-20 cm/s), flames survived at 14% O2, below the Earth limit of 16.5%.
BASS-II noted flamelets in orbit: tests T4 and T5. In T5 a small, dim flamelet seemed to burn the full sample length at very low airflow.
In NASA Glenn ground tests simulating microgravity, flamelets that survived low airflow quickly grew into a large fire when ventilation increased.

recommendations.strength: Turning the flow down was the experiment's procedure, so these counts show that stopping the air puts flames out, not how often a real fire would be stopped. The flare-up on restart was seen in ground tests that simulate microgravity, not yet in orbit.

recommendations.title: Qualify smoke detectors with real flaming smoke and lunar dust
recommendations.action: Test habitat detectors against smoke from flaming materials and against lunar dust, not only heated-sample smoke.

evidence.text: All 109 SAME-R smoke measurements come from heated, non-flaming samples.
On Mir (15 October 1994) a jumpsuit used to smother a small fire kept burning unnoticed and burned through; NASA notes it could have grown undetected into a large fire.
DAFT tested hand-held aerosol instruments aboard the ISS on a test dust (Arizona Road Dust) in 2 sessions; no PSI table measures how detectors respond to dust.
Carbon monoxide readings reached 950 ppm in BASS-II test O13a, and the CO sensor (range 0-1,000 ppm, BASS-II report p. 6) went over its range in 3 tests, so gas sensing can add a second signal.

recommendations.strength: The gap is certain; how detectors would perform is not measured in PSI.

spot_check.result: 10 of 10 match the report pages in content. One (M5) was a shortened quote without ellipses; it and three other shortened notes (M10, M16, T1) are now marked with '…'.

disagree.report: HCl O, only brief ignition, flame extinguished

cross_check.rule: PSI table 'Air display' cell says 'blowoff' or 'ext'; the category from the report must say the same.

anomaly_descriptions.sensor_failure: B2: final O2 of 1.6% and no frames; the test matrix notes 'cable came loose'.
anomaly_descriptions.implausible_o2_reading: Final O2 far outside the initial value for one burn: a sensor fault or a reading not taken. Excluded from statistics.
anomaly_descriptions.baseline_co_offset: Carbon monoxide recorded below zero: the sensor's zero point sits below zero.
anomaly_descriptions.raw_percent_typo: Oxygen written as 3400% or 2100%; read as 34% and 21%.
anomaly_descriptions.raw_thickness_typo: Thickness written as '037 mm'; read as 0.37 mm.
anomaly_descriptions.zero_pressure_outlier: Ambient pressure recorded as 0.0 mmHg, which is a vacuum.
anomaly_descriptions.material_filled_forward: Material cell was blank, meaning 'same as the row above'.
anomaly_descriptions.material_inferred: Material not written in this row; inferred from the same task's other rows.
anomaly_descriptions.material_not_stated: Neither the table nor NASA's test matrix names this sample's material.
anomaly_descriptions.embedded_footnote: Row is a footnote explaining the table, not a test.
anomaly_descriptions.pre_test_flow_visualisation: Pre-test airflow check, not a burn.
anomaly_descriptions.duplicate_row: This row repeats an earlier row in the same file.
anomaly_descriptions.duplicate_row_block: Part of a block of rows duplicated in the source file.
anomaly_descriptions.maintenance_row: A hardware maintenance log entry, not a test.
anomaly_descriptions.date_year_typo: The year in this date is inconsistent with its neighbours.
anomaly_descriptions.negative_flow_reading: Air flow recorded as negative: instrument drift near zero.
anomaly_descriptions.telemetry_loss: Time column records a signal loss instead of a clock time.
anomaly_descriptions.time_format_variant: Time written with dots instead of colons.
anomaly_descriptions.non_numeric_frame_count: Frame count holds a word such as 'none' or 'video'.
anomaly_descriptions.sensor_over_range: A gas reading exceeded its measurable range ('OR').
anomaly_descriptions.unreadable_cell: Cell contains bytes that could not be decoded.
anomaly_descriptions.zero_ignition_day: A full test day on which no flame ignited.
anomaly_descriptions.flow_recorded_as_fan_setting_only: Only a fan setting was logged, so no calibrated airspeed is given.
anomaly_descriptions.geometry_from_sample_group: Shape taken from other rows with the same sample number.
anomaly_descriptions.o2_recorded_as_range: Oxygen written as a range; the lower end is used for filtering.
anomaly_descriptions.unit_inconsistency_across_tables: SIBAL thickness is 0.37 cm / 0.33 cm in SAFFIRE-I/III but 0.37 mm in SAFFIRE-II.
anomaly_descriptions.dimension_order_inconsistency: Sample length and width are swapped between SAFFIRE-I and SAFFIRE-III.
anomaly_descriptions.header_unit_mismatch: Column says 'Spread Length' but holds rates in mm/s.
anomaly_descriptions.inconsistent_ignition_record: Hot ignition recorded 'No' yet a burn time and termination are recorded.

science_flag_descriptions.cool_flame_territory: Heptane droplet above 2.4 mm: conditions where FLEX found invisible cool-flame burning can continue after visible extinction. A territory marker, not an observation recorded for this test.
science_flag_descriptions.cool_flame_mentioned_in_comment_only: The comment describes a cool flame but the 'Cool flame?' column is empty, so it is not counted as recorded.

outcome_labels.extinguished_flow_stopped: Put out by stopping the airflow

transcription_note: BASS-II outcomes and flow directions were transcribed from the test matrices in NASA/TM-20210011385 Appendix A (pp. 103-113) with AI assistance. Each record cites its page so it can be checked; the summary category is this project's reading of NASA's words, which are shown verbatim.
